chunks: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Babawayh (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated, saying: He informed us, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Jahm ibn Abi Jahm, who said:

I saw Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both) after he had prostrated following the three rak'ahs of Maghrib. I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I saw you prostrate after the three [rak'ahs].' He said, 'And did you see me?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Then do not leave it, for indeed supplication in it is answered.'

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a common phrase of respect)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and significance of prostrating after the three rak'ahs of Maghrib prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the Sunnah of performing a prostration of gratitude (Sujud al-Shukr) or extended prostration immediately after the three rak'ahs of Maghrib, a practice attributed to Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS). The Imam’s concise confirmation, 'And did you see me?', underscores the authenticity of the observation, while the specific mention that supplication is answered during this moment highlights its spiritual efficacy as a time for direct divine response.
